steps.title: Read the question – extract the ‘givens’, decide the tools
steps.description:
•  Demand curve (in direct form):   q(4+p²)=10 ⇒ q(p)=10/(4+p²)
•  Revenue: R(p)=p·q(p)
•  Price–elasticity formula:  E(p)=-(dq/dp)(p/q)
•  Linear inverse–supply: p^{S}(q)=αq+β, with equilibrium (q*,p*)=(2,4)
•  Producer surplus at the equilibrium is 2.

Relevant Mathematical Methods material
(1)  Functions & Differentiation – rewrite and differentiate q(p) and R(p).
(2)  One–variable optimisation – use the first derivative to find where R is ↑/↓.
(3)  Integration – compute producer surplus (an area under a curve).
(4)  Systems of linear equations – solve simultaneously for α and β.

steps.title: Differentiate the demand curve and build the elasticity formula
steps.description:
Write q(p)=10(4+p²)^{-1}.
Find dq/dp using the chain rule:
  dq/dp =10·(-1)(4+p²)^{-2}·2p = -20p/(4+p²)².
Insert into E(p)=-(dq/dp)(p/q):
  E(p)= -(-20p)(p)/(4+p²)² / [10/(4+p²)]
        = 20p²(4+p²)/(10(4+p²)²)
        = 2p²/(4+p²).
steps.hints: A neat cancellation of one power of (4+p²) occurs – watch the algebra.

steps.title: Show that the elasticity never exceeds 2
steps.description:
For p≥0,
  E(p)=2p²/(4+p²).
Observe  0≤p²<4+p²  ⇒  0≤p²/(4+p²)<1.
Multiply by 2:  0≤E(p)<2.
Hence price elasticity of demand is always below the value 2 and never exceeds it.
steps.hints: Compare numerator and denominator directly instead of differentiating E(p) once more.

steps.title: Construct the revenue function and locate its turning point
steps.description:
Revenue: R(p)=p·q(p)=10p/(4+p²).
Differentiate (quotient rule or product rule with a power):
  dR/dp = 10(4+p²)^{-1} + 10p(-1)(4+p²)^{-2}·2p
         = 10/(4+p²) - 20p²/(4+p²)².
Put over a common denominator (4+p²)²:
  dR/dp = [10(4+p²) - 20p²]/(4+p²)²
         = 10(4-p²)/(4+p²)².
Sign of dR/dp depends on 4-p²:
  •  If p<2, derivative >0 ⇒ revenue is increasing.
  •  If p>2, derivative <0 ⇒ revenue is decreasing.
Thus revenue starts to fall once price rises above 2.
steps.hints: The critical price 2 equals the point where the numerator 4-p² changes sign.

steps.title: Approximate the revenue change when price rises 1 → 1.1
steps.description:
Use the tangent-line (linear) approximation ΔR≈R'(1)·Δp with Δp=0.1.
We already have dR/dp =10(4-p²)/(4+p²)².
At p=1:  dR/dp =10(4-1)/(4+1)² =30/25 =1.2.
Therefore   ΔR ≈ 1.2·0.1 = 0.12.
Interpretation: raising the price from £1 to £1.10 is expected to increase revenue by roughly £0.12 per unit time period (same units as R).
steps.hints: The method is exactly the ‘use the derivative to approximate a function’ learning outcome.

steps.title: Impose the equilibrium and producer-surplus conditions on supply
steps.description:
Inverse supply: p^{S}(q)=αq+β.
1.  Market equilibrium (q*,p*)=(2,4):  4 = α·2 + β.  (Eq. 1)
2.  Producer surplus at equilibrium equals 2.  For a linear supply
    PS = ∫₀^{q*} [p* - p^{S}(q)] dq
       = ∫₀^{2} [4 - (αq+β)] dq
       = ∫₀^{2} (4-β-αq) dq
       = (4-β)q - (α/2)q² |₀^{2}
       = 2(4-β) - 2α.
   Set equal to 2:  2(4-β) - 2α = 2 ⇒ 4 - β - α = 1.  (Eq. 2)
Solve the linear system (Eq. 1)–(Eq. 2):
  Eq. 1: 2α + β = 4
  Eq. 2:  α + β = 3
Subtract ⇒ α = 1. Substitute back ⇒ β = 2.
Hence the supply curve is  p^{S}(q)= q + 2.
steps.hints: You are using matrix/linear-equation skills implicitly – two equations, two unknowns.

final_solution:
1.  Price elasticity of demand generated by q(4+p²)=10 is
      E(p)=2p²/(4+p²), which for all p≥0 satisfies 0≤E(p)<2; therefore it never exceeds 2.

2a.  Revenue as a function of price is R(p)=10p/(4+p²).
    Its derivative is dR/dp =10(4-p²)/(4+p²)².
    Revenue rises for 0<p<2 and falls for p>2.

2b.  Using the derivative at p=1 (dR/dp=1.2) the approximate change when the price moves from 1 to 1.1 is
      ΔR ≈ 1.2·0.1 = 0.12.

3.  With inverse supply p^{S}(q)=αq+β, equilibrium (2,4) gives 2α+β=4.
    Producer surplus of 2 adds the condition α+β=3.
    Solving yields α=1, β=2, so the supply curve is p^{S}(q)=q+2.
